title: Lesson 8: Marriage and Relationships
description: Marriage is not finding a finished statue. It is two people who see what Jesus is making in each other and trust each other with the chisel. You will see the covenant love God gives first, how Christ's love for His church shapes marriage in Ephesians 5, and why drawing near to God draws two people near to each other.

blocks.text: You have spent this course learning to love the people around you: your neighbors, your family, and your church family. This lesson looks at the love that holds your closest relationships together. It is called covenant love, and it starts with the way God has already loved you.

blocks.alt: A husband handing his wife a chisel beside a rough block of marble, where a figure is beginning to emerge from the stone

blocks.title: The Marble and the Chisel
blocks.text:
A master sculptor does not walk into the quarry looking for a statue. He looks at a rough block of stone and sees what it could become. That is closer to how the Bible talks about love than anything we see in movies.

Nobody goes looking for a rough block of stone. We look for the finished statue, the person who already has it together. But there is no finished statue. There is only marble, and a Sculptor still at work. Marriage is not finding someone who has arrived. It is looking at a rough block of stone and seeing what Jesus is making in it.

And here is the harder part. In marriage you hand the other person your chisel. You let them see your pride, your selfishness, your rough edges, and you trust God to use them to shape you. A chisel in loving hands is patient. It is never a license to wound.
That kind of trust does not come naturally. Most of us protect ourselves and keep score. The courage to hand someone your chisel comes from knowing how God has already loved you.

Sometimes the person holding the chisel is struggling with the very thing they are pointing out in you. When that happens, the instinct is to reach for your own chisel and point back. But you did not hand them the chisel because they had arrived. You handed it to them because you both belong to the Sculptor. Truth is still true when it comes from someone who is also being shaped. Maturity is being able to say thank you.
8.1 - How do you feel about handing someone your chisel?
Covenant Love Starts with God
A covenant is a promise that does not depend on the other person.

When God made His covenant with Abram, He told him to prepare the ceremony, and then a deep sleep fell on Abram. In the dark, a smoking fire pot and a flaming torch passed between the pieces. Only God walked the path. Abram slept through the moment his own future was secured. God took the whole weight of the promise on Himself.
At the cross, Jesus did the same for you. He paid for your sin before you did anything, and He called His death the new covenant in His blood.

This is why the promises in a wedding are called vows and not terms. A contract says, I will, if you will. It keeps score, and it lasts only as long as the other person performs. A vow says, I will, even when. You make your vow to your spouse before God, and you keep it whether or not they keep theirs. That is an unconditional vow.
Covenant love has a shape, and it is not a straight line between two people.
Two people do not grow close by trying harder. They grow close as each one draws near to God. You give covenant love because you have first received it.
8.2 - How does your relationship with God change the way you love the person closest to you?
Marriage: Christ's Love on Display

Paul begins with a word for every Christian: submitting to one another out of reverence for Christ. Before anyone talks about roles, everyone bows low before Jesus. And this is where the vow does its work. Submission that waits its turn is not submission. It is negotiation. Unconditional love means you go first, and you keep going first, whether or not it is returned.

Paul asks wives to submit to their husbands as to the Lord, and to respect them. Biblical submission is not inferiority, silence, passivity, or following someone into sin. It is honoring and helping a husband under Jesus.
Then Paul gives his longest words to husbands, and they may be the hardest of all.
Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her,

Jesus did not wait for His bride to become lovely before He loved her. He did not wait for a finished statue. He gave Himself for her while she was still wandering. So a husband's leadership is measured by his sacrifice, not his control. If you promised you would die for her, you can lay down your pride for her today. Go first in serving, first in saying I was wrong, and first in giving up your comfort for her good.
Every Season Can Be Faithful

Maybe you are single, dating, or engaged. Maybe you are divorced, widowed, raising children on your own, blending two families, or in a hard marriage. God does not treat any of these seasons as a waiting room. Paul, who was unmarried, called singleness a gift with a special freedom for "undivided devotion to the Lord" (1 Corinthians 7:7, 35).

Marriage is a gift, but it is not the destination. Jesus lived the fullest human life that has ever been lived, and He never married. When Paul reaches the end of Ephesians five, the marriage he calls a profound mystery is Christ and the church. That is the marriage every other marriage points to, and it is the one that lasts.
So if you are single, you are not waiting for your life to begin. The Sculptor is already at work on you, and the church is where that shaping happens.
Keeping the Vow

Most of the time, keeping your vow will not look dramatic. It will look like forgiving something small on an ordinary Tuesday. A contract keeps a record, because the record is what protects you. A vow lets the record go, again and again, because you are not holding the promise together by yourself. This is where I will, even when stops being words you said once and becomes the way you live.
8.3 - Where is God asking you to go first: in forgiveness, in sacrifice, or somewhere else?
Lesson 8 Review

Marriage is not finding a finished statue. It is two people who see what Jesus is making in each other and trust each other with the chisel. That trust grows from covenant love, and covenant love always comes from God first. A contract says, I will, if you will. A vow says, I will, even when. As each person draws near to God, they draw near to each other.

And the chisel turns out not to be a blade at all. Christ did not wait for a finished statue. While we were still sinners, He died for us, because He saw what His love could make of us. Sacrificial love is the chisel. It is what shaped you, and it is what He gives you to hand to the person closest to you.
In the next lesson, you will learn how to protect that closeness when temptation pulls you away from God.

blocks.title: What covenant love is not
content: Covenant love is patient with ordinary weakness and ordinary hard days. It is not a promise to stay in danger. Ephesians 5 calls a husband to lay down his life, never to control, threaten, or harm, and biblical submission never means following someone into sin or accepting abuse. God never asks you to cover for someone who is hurting you or your children, and keeping your promises does not make you responsible for another person's sin.

If someone is harming, threatening, or controlling you, please tell a pastor or another safe, trusted person and get help. If you are in immediate danger, call 911 or your local emergency number. In the United States you can also call the National Domestic Violence Hotline at 1-800-799-7233.
